utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We had a bit of a late start, which was also caused by quite a bit of confusion in relation to whether or not Mr. Stanisic had waived his right to be present in court today. Let's start, perhaps, with that point. The Chamber received recently an update report from the forensic psychiatrist. The Chamber also received recently a new report on gastroenterology as we requested to be provided on those points. This morning, the Chamber received a weekly update report by Dr. Eekhof. Although it is not visible from this report, the Chamber inquired into whether Dr. Eekhof had seen Mr. Stanisic today, so as to be sure that the weekly report would include any observations of today. Then the Chamber received copies of a -- two forms, one in which Mr. Stanisic waived his right to be present, although he did not feel well enough to attend court, and the other one was the observations made in this respect, or rather formal report by the UNDU staff. Now, it turns out that the -- Mr. Stanisic made a mistake when he declared that he would waive his right to be present in court; is that correct, Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is, indeed, the information we received at 1.45 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one would expect the forms to be known by now, having been used several times, but that's the situation. The Chamber, meanwhile, asked the Senior Legal Officer to get in touch with the United Nations Detention Unit, and we understand that Mr. Stanisic has filled in the forms in such a way that he still feels not well enough to attend court, that does not waive his right to be present in court and that he does not wish to use the facilities to follow the proceedings through a video-conference link. Is that also in line with your information, Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Under the circumstances as they are known to the Chamber by now, the Chamber will proceed. Yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, does the Chamber means with proceeding that the Chamber's not willing to hear the comments of the Defence with respect to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one has asked me to give any comments on the matter. If you would like to give comments --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you could have asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to make such comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I explained that we would like to comment procedurally on the presence of the accused before the start of the case, if that is confusing, then my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you mean at an earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so. Could you give us an indication as to how much time you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a few minutes, if Your Honours may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you mean now to express the position of the Defence in view of starting the presentation of evidence by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In light of the absence of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence is in possession of the report of Dr. De Man and the preceding report of Dr. Eekhof in which he acknowledged -- acknowledges in his report of the 23rd of June that the general conclusion was that the health problems present a great complexity. This was based on a multidisciplinary meeting apparently which took place last week in the detention unit. This morning, we received the report of Dr. De Man, and in light of this report, we have no other option than to ask the Chamber to consider an adjournment of the proceedings, because we believe that the defendant is not capable of either participants here in the courtroom or through the videolink conference. The reason being that Dr. De Man clearly states in his report that the defendant considers his present life situation to be not worth living, and the examination shows sign of a major depression. Notably, Dr. De Man observes that there is no divergence between his opinion and that of his colleagues in Belgrade in -- on this issue. And in light of these circumstances, although the report we have to submit is not quite detailed of Dr. De Man, we think it's not in accordance with the rights of the accused to continue on the basis of this report. Now, my colleague, Mr. Jordash, has indicated to the Chamber some specific questions we would like to submit to Dr. De Man, which, in detail, would go into the question of the effective participation. This -- these questions were not taken into account and were not addressed by Dr. De Man, but apart from that, we believe that this information cannot be ignored in terms of its -- its I think very clear conclusion. In other words, a defendant who is considering suicide I think is hardly possibly to effectively participate in the proceedings. So on the basis of this report, we as Defence felt obliged to submit this application to the Court, or in the alternative, seek further clarification of Dr. De Man as to his conclusions. We as Defence, we're under the presumption that Dr. De Man would address the vital questions in this case for our position, namely whether we can continue as Defence in receiving any instructions, whether we can uphold a fair trial for this defendant, and that's the reason why we have submitted those questions to the Chamber. And now these questions were not taken into account. We receive a general report of Dr. De Man, which in itself is alarming, we believe, in itself; and in light of this report, we cannot continue as Defence with a defendant who is -- who is thinking of committing suicide and suffers from a major depression, and this is directly the dilemma the Defence is facing like last year. Apart from this whole situation of our position, we still believe that on the basis of this report it cannot be said by itself that this defendant is mentally fit to be present here today or participate through the videolink, and this is, I think, exactly the purpose why Dr. De Man was involved. So our application to the Chamber is primarily to adjourn the proceedings on the basis of this report. Secondly, in the alternative, seek further clarification as to the ramifications of what Dr. De Man means with the major depression, risk of suicide, the effects of sedative medication which are now reduced. But all those indicators clearly emphasise the presumption that this defendant is not fit to come to court or participate through the videolink or effective participation. This is our submission, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Brehmeier-Metz, would you like to make any observations in response to the submissions by Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREHMEIER-METZ
utterances.text: Indeed I would, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution would oppose the Defence application for an adjournment of the proceedings, and the Prosecution does not agree with Mr. Knoops's assessment of Dr. De Man's report. Indeed, there is nothing in the Prosecution's view in either the gastroenterologist's report or the most recent report of Dr. De Man to suggest that Jovica Stanisic cannot participate in today's proceedings. The ailments that were described by the gastroenterologist have been accommodated by the Chambers's decision on the trial modalities, and Dr. De Man describes Mr. Stanisic as being, and I quote: "cooperative, well-oriented, and quite alert, as showing no evident disturbances of memory, no disturbances of perception and judgement or thought disturbances, no hallucinatory experiences." In fact, there is something in Dr. De Man's report that suggests a district possibility that Mr. Stanisic is malingering and actually trying to manipulate the expert's findings. Dr. De Man describes that he was shown a UNDU recording that shows Mr. Stanisic moving around in his cell without problems and that he seemingly applied a substance, possibly cigarette ash, under his lower eyelids. Initially when Dr. De Man visited Mr. Stanisic, he claimed that he was too tired to proceed with the interview with Dr. De Man and that claim seemed to be supported by, as Dr. De Man notes, the grey discolouration under eyes. After a break, those marks were done. The recording shown to Dr. De Man clearly indicates that the discolouration was not a sign of Mr. Stanisic's claimed tiredness but that he applied those marks himself in order to deceive Dr. De Man. The Prosecution has since asked that the Registry make the recording that was shown to Dr. De Man available also to the parties in this case, and as soon as this request is granted, we will inform the Defence accordingly so that they, too, can watch it. For today's proceedings, though, I can only repeat what I said initially, namely that there is no evident medical reason why Mr. Stanisic should not be present in the courtroom or in the video-conference link room and that the trial should proceed accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, any need to -- or Mr. Jordash, any need to briefly respond to what was said by Ms. Brehmeier-Metz.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just very briefly. The issue at its simplest is that Dr. De Man's report is simply not detailed enough. We will, in our respectful submission, keep coming back to the same debate, because the psychiatric evidence we keep receiving doesn't address the specific questions. We, the Defence, would, like everyone in this room, like to get on with this trial. We, the Defence, are faced with a psychiatric report, which despite our best efforts, doesn't address the key fitness questions. Now, if it be right that Mr. Stanisic was rubbing ash in his -- on his lower eyelid, then, yes, an inference arises of malingering, but an inference also arises of simply odd behaviour that Mr. Stanisic would think, one, that that was an effective route. Two, as I understand the situation, Dr. De Man had a break, and when he returned the ash or the greyness was removed. So if it was a ruse by Mr. Stanisic, it was a rather ridiculous one, because he removed the ash before Dr. De Man came back, knowing Dr. De Man was coming back. So we keep returning to malingering, odd behaviour, and serious depression. We, the Defence, are faced constantly with serious depression and an inability to be able to approach the accused with confidence, that when we do so, he understands what is occurring and can participate in giving us instructions. So all we have been trying to endeavour to do is get enough details so we can avoid these backwards and forwards discussions with the Prosecution as to whether Mr. Stanisic is malingering or not; and, two, know what we, the Defence, can do when approaching somebody, and this isn't disputed it would seem, when approaching somebody who appears to have suicidal thoughts. Do we keep approaching him for instructions knowing that he may get worse and may -- it may increase his desire to commit suicide, or do we simply turn up to court without instructions? It's that which the Defence are trying to request the Court assist us with to a degree, to provide us with the detail that would allow us to do our job. Those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Before we continue -- yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist the Court. I do fully acknowledge the observations of the Prosecution, but if Your Honours may also look at paragraph 2 of the report of Dr. Eekhof, it's saying, which is never stated by him before, that the discrepancy between the physical claims by Mr. Stanisic and the view of the -- of Dr. Eekhof, he said, "can be explained by -- as neurotic behaviour." So in other words, we can't exclude the possibility that we are dealing with a person who is that ill that it also affects his abilities in terms of his non-neurotic behaviour; and if the observation would lead to the conclusion that he is putting cigarette ash on his face, it can very well be an exponent of this neurotic behaviour, and that's why my learned friend says we, as Defence, we simply would like to have further clarification as to the level of participation and instructions this defendant can give us or not give us before we can clearly provide him the best Defence as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a few questions. Was there any medical report over the last year which clearly, unambiguously, established that Mr. Stanisic, at the time that report was made, was unfit to stand trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I -- since the accused -- since the trial was adjourned last year, I don't think there has been a report which has unambiguously stated that, but the question has never been asked. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has it been raised that he's unfit to stand trial by you, by the Defence, because under the normal circumstances, a trial does not start by establishing that someone is fit to stand trial. That's the normal situation. And we have heard a lot of doubts expressed on whether he was fit to stand trial, but is there any unambiguous motion to say -- declare him unfit to stand trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, if I could answer that in this way, that during the adjournment, we didn't seek to push that point because the trial wasn't proceeding at that point. So we were keen to ensure that Mr. Stanisic's treatment could continue without triggering off that procedure which necessarily involves the Prosecution's instruction of experts, the Defence instructions of experts, which would have necessarily interrupted what we understood to be a fairly rigorous and sensitive therapeutic regime in Belgrade. Upon -- at some point, the date escapes me, but two months ago or so, Mr. Stanisic was then recalled. Think it's fair to say that was a surprise to us and it was a surprise to the Prosecution, because the Prosecution were not asking for him to be recalled for trial, they were asking him to be recalled for diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment you are explaining, perhaps, I do not know yet where you're going, why things happened as they happened. My question is simple, that is: Was there any unambiguous request for this Chamber to establish that on the basis of the medical information Mr. Stanisic is unfit to stand trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was just arriving at that point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic was recalled, and we have been seeking, since then, to have a report deal with the very questions which would be the basis of such an application. This is why we sent fairly detailed questions to your legal officer, so that the report produced by Dr. De Man would address the questions and we would know whether there was a basis for fitness issue or not. If not, then we would have been able to save court time by not raising the issue every time we get to the start of a new proceedings, which we -- of course, irritates us and I'm sure irritates everybody else too. It's that lack of information which means we cannot let the point drop, nor can we pursue it. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Has the situation in relation to the major depression, has it -- are there clear signs that it has changed over the last three months?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps I can answer that in this way, that I've seen Mr. Stanisic, and Mr. Knoops, and other members of the team have seen him, and I think it's fair to say that his observable symptoms from a lay perspective appear to be getting worse, but whether they, in fact, reflect a worsening of his condition, we don't know. We can only say it as we see it as lay people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then perhaps I should have been more precise in my question. Do the medical reports reflect a considerable change, substantial change, as far as the major depression is concerned over the last three months?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In our -- in our submission, they would appear to -- I think they appear to be slightly at odds with each other. Dr. Petrovic appears to suggest the condition is the same as the accused's condition was in Belgrade. Dr. Eekhof appears to suggest that there's been an improvement. Dr. De Man's latest report seems to be ambiguous. On the one hand an improvement of judgement, but on the other hand, new symptoms of suicidal ideation. So it's a rather mixed bag of medical results in our submission arising from the lack of specificity of the medical records, reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber decides that the request for an adjournment of the trial at this moment is denied, and the reasons for this decision will be put on the record soon. I would now like to move to a matter which has not yet been resolved, that is, protective measures for the witness to be called, and I'd like to turn into private session, which I think in this courtroom also needs the curtains to be pulled down.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We have dealt with the protective measures to be granted to the present witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes past 4.00, and we'll then actually start the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we proceed, Mr. Hoffmann, he'd like to inform the parties already that a decision has been filed this afternoon in which the motion for bifurcation of the evidence was denied. Mr. Hoffmann, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness C-015, you'll now be examined by Mr. Hoffmann. Mr. Hoffmann is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall giving a statement to investigators from this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would ask that the document 65 ter 5030 be brought on the monitor. This is a statement dated 10, 11 and 13 May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Mr. C-015, on the screen before you, you can see a document purporting to be a statement given by you on 10, 11 and 13 May 1999. Do you recall giving a statement on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom of that page at the signature, do you recognise this as your own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session, isn't it? Yes, because you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, I think some credit due on the part of Madam Registrar is in place that what is now on the screen has not been broadcasted. You should specifically ask for this not to be broadcasted, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. If we could please go to page 10 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And again, Witness, I've asked you to look at the signature and to tell the Court whether that's your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Could we now see, please, document 65 ter 5032 on the screen. It's a statement given on 24 January 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you wanted to add, And it should also not be shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And again, Witness, I ask you to look at the signature of -- on that page, whether you recognise this as your own.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just finally if we can go to page 6 of the English document, and the same question would be for that page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: There it is. Whether you recognise that signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature. I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And, Witness, did you have a chance to -- prior to coming to testify to review both of these statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to put down in writing any changes or clarifications you made to those two statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were a few corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can I just ask that 65 ter 5029 be brought up on the screen. That is, in fact, a table of clarifications that the witness made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It should not be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And again, Witness, if you look at that table, do you recognise your signature at the bottom of that table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And just for the completeness of the record, if we can go to the last page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: The document should consist of three pages. If need be and to expedite the proceedings, we do have a hard copy to be shown to the witness if that would be easier. And just for the record, Your Honours, we have provided the Defence with that same table this morning through e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And I would ask you, Witness, if you just look at the document, at the signature of -- on each page and just quickly confirm whether it's your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Are these all the clarifications you wanted to make to the two statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And subject to these corrections in the document before you, did your statements that you signed in 1999 and 2001 accurately reflect what you told the Prosecutor's office at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And final question: If you were asked the same questions today that were asked in 1999 and 2001, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point in time I would ask that both the statements be admitted into evidence, that is, 65 ter 5030, in the first place. That is the 1999 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Apart from the objections which were raised against the use of 92 ter statements in general, which was, I think, specifically with Witness C-015. That's already a while ago that you responded to -- to several motions by the Prosecution to have 92 ter statements introduced into evidence. Mr. Jovanovic, you are arguing that it would be unfair to have a written statement and at the same time have -- have oral testimony to be given. And, Mr. Knoops, the Stanisic Defence had some other problems. Any objections at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you. Other than the ones that we have already stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No further objections at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that the objections stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please assign numbers to all three documents. Let's start with the 1999 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement 65 ter 5030 will become Exhibit P2, under seal. Statement 65 ter 5032 will become Exhibit P3 under seal, and 65 ter number 5029 will become Exhibit P4, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And all three of them are admitted into evidence, under seal. Please proceed, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And for the public record, we also prepared redacted versions of each of the documents, and we would ask that those be admitted as well into evidence. The 1999 statement is 65 ter 5031, as redacted version, the 2001 statement is redacted as 65 ter 5033, and the table of clarifications in redacted form is 65 ter Exhibit 5034.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has not been provided with those before. It's mainly a matter of carefully checking whether the redactions are sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any observations from the Defence teams? If not, the Chamber decides that they will be marked for identification so as to enable the Chamber to have a closer look to it. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P5, P6, and P7, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the thing we'll also consider, well, whether all redacted versions will always have to be admitted into evidence because the evidence doesn't change a bit. Of course, it's important to have these exhibits to be made known to the public, but we'll further consider that as well. For the time being, they're MFI'd as P5, P6, and P7. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would now ask that we briefly go into closed session for a few remarks on the personal background of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Before I start with some questions regarding the events in the region of Eastern Slavonia, I would like to show you a map from the court binder of maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would ask the Court Officer to place map number 7 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please refer to the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes. The 65 ter number is listed as CB-map 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, if you have a look at the map in front of you on the screen, do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: What does this map depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Republika Srpska Krajina is shown on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, is this an accurate and official map of the RSK at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to -- you to indicate to the Court the three areas of the Serb Autonomous Region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and if you would take the pen with the Court Usher's assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have a code for the colour of marking? I would like any marking to be made during this trial in one colour for the Prosecution and another colour for the Defence, so as to be able to make a distinction if any marking was made on the request of one party or the other. Now, the choice is blue and red. Mr. Hoffmann, any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: No preference on my side, but to expedite, I would go for red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Red for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, if you could mark the area of Baranja with a capital B, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where the Dunav flows into -- the Drava flows into the Danube. That is where the border is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if I could ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up towards the Hungarian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if I could ask you now to mark the area of Slavonia with a capital S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Danube River up to this narrowing here. That's Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And finally, would ask you to indicate the area of Western Srem with a capital WS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this narrowing here down to the border with Serbia. That is the area of Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'd ask that these markings be saved, and I would tender this map with the markings of Witness C-015 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7 -- P8, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Not to be expected. P7 it be admitted into evidence, can be a part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I think it's Exhibit P8, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, P8. Yes, then I misspoke. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And I would ask, actually, the following map, which is map 7A, just contains the translation of the text on this map, that this would be included in the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's usually if an exhibit is admitted into evidence, the translation is uploaded into e-court and is automatically also admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I wonder why we needed the witness to find out where these locations are on a map. It seems to be something you could easily agree upon, and I do not think that this witness has any opinion different on the matter than any other witness would have. So therefore, it certainly would have been a matter to compromise upon if there was any need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: We certainly will do so for the future, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would now ask that we quickly look at map 18. It has a similar 65 ter number, CB-Map 18. This is, in fact, just a closer map of the region of the SAO SBWS. Taking upon your suggestion, I would simply ask if there are any objections from the Defence or whether we can simply tender this map into evidence. It's just a matter of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any disagreement that this map depicts what was said already by Mr. Hoffmann a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this map can be assigned a number. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P9, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P9 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in your statement from 1999, Exhibit P2, you do mention a training centre in Erdut, and you say it was used for the Territorial Defence, the TO, prior to August 1991. What happened to that training centre after 1st August 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the centre was placed under our control, we took the weapons from there, infantry weapons, rifles, M-48s. There were several automatic rifles, protective masks also, Thomson guns - it's an old type of weapon - and also a combat kit of 100 pieces of ammunition for each of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And by whom was that training centre used after 1st August 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 1991, it was used by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Was it used by the police all the time in 1991, or was it later used by other?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Well, then, I simply stick to the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Was it used by the police all the time in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police did not use it that whole time. When Arkan came, he threw the police out, and then he moved into the centre, and he was there until the peaceful reintegration. And then three months later, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina came back, and then he went to a different location downstream of the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned a person by the name Arkan. Can you tell the Court his full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And who was that Arkan, Zeljko Raznjatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember him from football matches of the Red Star Crvena Zvezda. He was arrested once in Croatia, and then he was released. This is also what I remember. And I remember him coming to Tenja. And as I said before, when he later chucked the police out and he, himself, moved into that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: In what relation did Arkan stand to the JNA, the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the proper way of asking this question. Was there any relation, and then to next question, what that relationship may have been. Now, I'm just checking on whether there's anything already in the statement about this. Mr. Knoops, is there any relationship between Arkan and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In such a specific way it was not asked to the witness in the statement, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But if in the statement as a basis for accepting that there was a relationship, then there's no need to object against leading. Please proceed, Mr. Hoffmann, but perhaps you do it, since we have not found yet the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If I may assist. It's actually in the 1999 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the 1999 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And page 3 of the English and the first full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: There is reference to the training centre it, and there is reference to the JNA, put it that way. It says that: "Weapons, ammunition, and other equipment was brought in to the training centre from the JNA storage."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so -- well, of course, you could say if it was brought in, it doesn't mean that there is a relationship but let's -- and of course, we have to get used to each other. Mr. Hoffmann, of course, to ask who Arkan is, if that was already in the statement is totally superfluous, because the statement says exactly who this witness thinks Arkan was. At the same time, let's not be over-technical. The leading, if it comes to a point where it would really be of importance, then, of course, there's nothing against objecting. However, if the route for the question already found in the statement, it could hardly still be considered a question which is based on an assumption which is not yet established, because this is already in evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, if you answer that question. In what relation did the -- did Arkan stand to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- no relation. In a word, they just didn't get along.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Was there any relation between Arkan and the local Serb government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I wasn't there, so I can't say, but where he was, the local population received him quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who Mile Ulemek was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mile Ulemek is a member of Arkan's guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: What about Milorad Stricevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milorad Stricevic is a person who appeared in our area and introduced himself as Colonel Milorad Stricevic. And there was also, at that time, a man in Belgrade in the then-secretariat, Federal Secretariat for National Defence, by the name of Stricevic until he was actually detected, and then he transferred himself to Arkan's unit as a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Now, in your 1999 statement, Exhibit P2, at page 5 in the English version, you refer to Mile Ulemek and Arkan in the relation to the arrest of a few Croats from Klisa in October 1991. Can you tell the Court what happened to these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we please moved into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into closed session. We rely that -- upon you, Witness C-015, that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we are now in open session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And I would ask the Court Officer to place 65 ter number 1881 on the screen for the witness. It is a report from the commander of the Dalj police station to the minister of the interior of the SAO SBWS, dated 23rd September, 1991. Its subject is the hand-over of prisoners from the Dalj police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the Prosecution is able to submit this document to the witness, we believe that there should first be made a foundation for introducing this document, as per also the guidelines in the Perisic case in paragraph 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, I hope you'll forgive me that I have not -- I think, as a matter of fact, I saw that you had you had an agreement during a recently-held meeting in which reference was made to the -- to the Perisic practice, which I'm not. And you said paragraph 27. Yes. Would that oppose against having this document being tendered from the bar table as well? Because often we find the direct link with the witness is not there, which would even cause a party to tender it not through a witness at all. Because apparently your problem is that it should not be tendered through this witness. Would there be any objection against it being tendered without a witness? Is there any concern about authenticity, or is there any ... Apart from another matter, you referred to -- yes. You pointed at that under this rule to have it introduced through this witness that a basis should be -- foundation should be laid for that. So apart from what the alternatives would be, Mr. Hoffmann, if you're able to lay such a foundation, you're invited to do so. If not, we'll see what other options there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I was to ask the witness about the document, which I think would lay the foundation. I'm asking him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And I don't have the Perisic guidelines at hand right now, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, you say before it's submitted. Does that mean in your view the witness should not even see the document in order to establish what the foundation is for this witness to testify about this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because that would amount to refreshment of memory, leading the witness by a document which is not authored by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, you can do it perhaps without showing it to the witness, and -- although the Chamber might not be over-technical, let's see where we go. Could you ask the witness such a question which would establish a link between him and this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I will certainly try, but I would have thought that the practice in this Tribunal is actually that he's allowed to have a look at the document and then talk about whether he knows the document and the content of the document, but I'll try to -- obviously without then referring even to the content of the document, to ask him about it. It seems to me, honestly, rather time-consuming. And in addition, I would like to note that this document has been previously admitted. So it seems to me that there is a presumption that it's been found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, I take it that it has been admitted in another case. The issue, apparently, is, and Mr. Knoops says this is not the way in which this document should be introduced. Admission in another case, maybe under different circumstances, with a different witness, with a different level of relevance, different probative value. We are in the very early stages of this proceedings, and apparently you want -- you intended to show to the witness a piece of correspondence addressed to the minister of the interior of the Autonomous Region Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem with -- in relation to the hand-over of prisoners. Witness C-015, are you familiar with correspondence of the kind as I just mentioned, that is, hand-over of prisoners, 1991? Are you familiar with documentation in relation to such transfer or hand-over of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me, in order to really resolve this problem very quickly I should like you -- ask to move into closed session, and I can clarify everything regarding these documents, and it will be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Any questions in relation to this document other than what the witness told us already, Mr. Hoffmann? And please keep in mind that this might be a sensitive issue in terms of protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, just what you told us about what happened to these people and how they were killed, how did you learn about it? And again if you feel that the answer to that question would reveal your identity, we would have to go back into private session. The question would be how do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will have to mention names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we return into closed session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And I would ask that the next document be placed on the monitor, which is 65 ter number 355.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: C-015, I would ask you to look at the document in front of you. It is an Official Note of the Dalj police station regarding incidents on the premises of that police station on 4, 5 October 1991. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the events described in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: How do you know about these events as described in the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person who wrote the statement told me that. I had the opportunity to spend some five or six years together with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If we can go on the B/C/S version to the bottom of the page, and in English to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If you look, Witness, at the persons who drafted that report, are you familiar with those two names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And what about the recipient of that report, which is listed on the left side at the bottom of the page under number 2? Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a little bit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: That would be the bottom part of the document, in the left corner. The second last line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness C-015, is your problem that you can't read it, or is it a problem that you have to think about whether you -- apparently Mr. Hoffmann is referring to what appears after 2, Mr. Hoffmann, where it reads "komandantu specijalne," and then can you read what then follows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot see now. I don't have my reading glasses. Unfortunately, they are up there. I didn't bring my reading glasses with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could that line -- first of all, could we have the whole screen with the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it clearer to you now? Could even be enlarged a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then repeat your question, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Again, Witness, if -- under number 2, can you tell us whether you are familiar with the name that is mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to us. He was in charge of setting up police stations in our area. He had come from Serbia with Badza. And it was his task to set up police stations in places where the police stations existed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Would you say that this report is correct and in line with your own knowledge of the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document 65 ter 355 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, before I ask whether any objections, "your own knowledge" is a rather ambiguous term in evidential -- in the evidential context. What is my own knowledge, that you are named Mr. Hoffmann? They told me. I've got no idea finally, and if I verified it, it's hearsay, which doesn't make it unreliable. What do you mean by this is a rather -- is a document with quite a few elements in it. When you say, "Is this in line with your own knowledge," do you mean hearsay reports on the same events, and if so, is it done by the same persons or by other persons? Because if the same persons who apparently gave this information told this witness the same story, that's different from knowing from other sources than those persons that the same. So I think it would be worthwhile to briefly explore that, because otherwise we might draw wrong conclusions. And I see the document now for the first time, apparently the witness not. I would like to read through it to see whether ... Perhaps while I'm reading you put -- if you have any questions to the witness, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, you told the Court before that you had talked to the chief of the police station, Cizmic, about these events. Do you have any other source of information regarding these events on 4 and 5 October 1991, in the Dalj police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that before. I don't have anything other than that and what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Maybe if you go to the last paragraph, Witness. There is mentioning that a number of persons are missing since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Maybe we can zoom in a bit on this last paragraph for the witness to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Have you been involved, witness, with any involvement with finding any of these persons or follow-up on these persons? And it may be that for this answer we again have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we go into closed session, Witness C-015? Then we'll move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We were about to hear whether there were any objections against admission into evidence of this document. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to this document being tendered as evidence because it contains various forms of double hearsay which in all reasonableness could not be within the knowledge of this witness. For instance, first page, at the second paragraph whereby reference is made to several telephone calls. It's at the end of paragraph of three, and more in particular, in page 2 where in the fourth, fifth, sixth line mention is made of a conversation that was heard, or at least words which were heard and which were attributed to an institution. I'm not reading that out for the record, but you'll find it on page 2, from the fifth line onwards. So if the Court would admit this document at all, we would submit that these portions could not be admitted, because there is no relation between the witness and the contents of those two portions in the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same reasons, Your Honour, that were stated by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considered the objection to be rather to wait for this contemporaneous document, which, of course, will be considered in the context of the totality of the evidence. The objection against admission is, therefore, overruled. Madam Registrar, this would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P11 is admitted into evidence. It's time for a break, Mr. Hoffmann. We will have a break of 20 minutes, and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In the interests of time, I will skip a couple parts of the examination-in-chief, because as I think Your Honour indicated, most of those things are to some extent covered in the statement. I would, therefore, go now to show a video-clip. It is 65 ter 4718. The clip is taken from the video ERN V000-3788, and it's starting at minutes 30:15 of the original tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any spoken text on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript has been provided to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: It has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I, again, to the extent that the speed of speech is such that it's impossible to follow that one of the interpreters verifies whether what is said appears on the transcript and that the other one takes the time necessary for interpretation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have -- where do I hear the English translation? I see it on the screen, but that's, of course, not on the transcript, and since the French translation is on channel 5, we have an incomplete record if we have no English translation. I don't know what channel I can receive that either --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the English booth does not usually read if the English is on the screen. We usually get a printed-out transcript then we can read. The way it is now, it is just too fast for us to follow and to verify that it actually is the translation of what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- I would say that is more or less the same for you as it is the French booth. So, therefore, the system and I think we try to do it in this way during the opening statement, the system being that one of interpreters checks whether the spoken words are the same as the words written and that then that means from B/C/S into English, and that the other interpreter just interprets rather than read what appears to be a translation of which, of course, the accuracy is -- well, thought to be established. Would that possible, because the French booth is apparently able to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the actual speech in B/C/S is too fast to be simultaneously interpreted. So we can read if we have the transcript, but at this pace it is not possible to verify that it will be an exact simultaneous translation. It's just too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there an original transcript, that means B/C/S, provided to the booth? THE PROSECUTOR: My understanding is all the booths were provided with a B/C/S original transcript and the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I then invite the English booth to verify whether the words spoken in B/C/S are the words as they appear in the B/C/S transcript, and that the other interpreter then interprets from the written B/C/S version. It's not then a simultaneous translation, and it may take two or three or four or five minutes longer. I also invite the Prosecution, if it's a very lengthy video-clip, then to stop half so that we can catch up. But if not, then the translation, I do understand that that's also how the French booth does it, is then a translation from a transcript in B/C/S which been checked upon whether it's an accurate transcript of the words spoken. Could we restart. If there's any further observation, I would like to hear. I would very much like to resolve the problems in -- together with you than --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Let me just -- for the information of the booth, the relevant clip in the transcript can be found on page 3, both English and B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that might assist they know where to find it on the transcript, because otherwise you start --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Again, my understanding was that we did provide those transcripts with an indication where the clips are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everybody tries to do their utmost best, and is this workable the way in which I suggested it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can do our best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- I'm -- that's what we know. Let's restart.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Reporter: Krajina is solemnly celebrating the day of security. On this day three days ago, the first large gathering of people and mass protests again the Croatian leadership took place in Knin. The result of those events was a petition signed by the policeman of the then-Knin Public Security -- Security Station refusing obedience to the pro-Ustasha authorities in Zagreb and refusing to wear markings worn by Ustashas 50 years ago while committing genocide against the Serbian people. The central celebration took place in Knin. Milan Martic, minister of the interior, spoke at the formal events stressing at the end of his speech that the chequer-board flag can be in Knin only over our dead bodies. Among speakers addressing the gathering were Goran Hadzic, President of the Knin Municipal Assembly. On the occasion of the day of security of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, there were issued Serbian rebellions now prizing decorations, medals for courage, and certificates of gratitude issued."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that you even tried to keep up with it. I do not mind if your translation finishes one minute after that. That's would not be no problem because I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The problem was that we actually didn't find the right place in the transcript, so we just had to go by what was on the screen, so we did our best to follow the pace there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then next time I'll invite the party who presents such a video-clip with a transcript to clearly indicate before we start where the beginning is to be found. I, nevertheless, admire the way you did it. Mr. Hoffmann, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness C-015, this was a television report of a ceremony on the RSK security service day on 5 July 1993. Have you seen this footage before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, just judging by the footage that you saw, where this ceremony was held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was held in Knin. This was the former JNA hall. It was then renamed the police hall, the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Did you in person attend this celebration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: On this video footage did you recognise any of the people attending the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised Goran Hadzic. I recognised Milan Novakovic, the late Babic. Mr. Stanisic is there also, I believe, Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: You say you believe Mr. Stanisic was there. If it helps you, we can certainly replay the clip if there is any doubt on your side whether he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about the persons appearing and whether Mr. Stanisic is among them? If so -- if there's no dispute, then -- Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to ask another question of a procedural nature. If the witness says that he did not attend the celebration, the presentation of a video -- of the video footage of some celebration means that it is possible in the future to show anyone any video-clip and ask for a comment. The witness, namely, clearly said that he did not attend it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But he may recognise features we are unfamiliar with but he is familiar with. If you'd show me a video of a mountain, I might not know what mountain it is, while someone who is living close to the Mont Blanc could tell us that for this and this and this reason, he recognises the Mont Blanc. So, therefore, it's not just asking for comment apparently from the answers of this witness, we learn that he is familiar with the location. Apparently, if you disagree, you can cross-examine him on the matter, and, apparently, he recognises quite a number of persons. Whereas, Mr. Hoffmann now tells us would we have to show it again in order to see whether Mr. Stanisic is there, but, apparently, Mr. Knoops does not seem to challenge that one of the persons shown during this meeting is Mr. Stanisic. Please proceed, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if there's any Simatovic challenge of Mr. Stanisic being shown, then of course we would like to hear so that we can play it again. I see Mr. Simatovic, although he's not giving evidence, is nodding no, and this is understood as instructing counsel not to challenge the presence of Mr. Stanisic. Is that well-understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's the reporter that's actually saying where the place is, where it is being held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can cross-examine the witness on how familiar he is with the location, and whether he's just repeating what the reporter says, or whether he has any personal knowledge of that location. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Actually, following on the discussion I would tender this clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P12, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Then P12 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness C-015, when I ask you whether you did attend this ceremony you said no, but another one. Was there any other celebration or ceremony that you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I attended another celebration. I went to see those people in my area who were at the school, but as I told you before, I'm not going to talk about it because it was not part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I was actually referring -- or let me rephrase my question, Witness. Did you ever see Jovica Stanisic in person, at any time, in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: At what occasion did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him on several occasions, but I repeat, we have talked about this. This is not in my statement, and I'm not going to talk about it. I do not wish to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are under an obligation to answer questions. It's not for the witness to decide what questions he wants to answer and what questions he doesn't want to answer. So, therefore, I invite you, if need be in closed session, if there's any -- if you would have any problem of the kind we discussed earlier, but it's not that you and Mr. Hoffmann together decide what questions will be answered. May I invite you to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Maybe I'll rephrase it, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Let me just rephrase my question, Witness C-015 when looking at this footage I did ask you whether you attended the ceremony in Knin, you said no but you did attend another similar meeting. Do you recall any such meeting in the area of Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about that meeting? Who was meeting, and who was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all right. If you insist, I'll tell you where I was. I went there, as I said, to tour the area, the people in the school, and Golubic. This is a place near Knin where policemen were being trained. You know that we were at war and that we did not have the necessary police personnel, so a training centre was set up there where one had existed previously in the former Yugoslavia, and it was set up to train police. I went there. I visited my people there. After I had visited them I left, and I -- there you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Did you, at any time, meet one of the accused in the area of Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was then only, and I saw Jovica Stanisic on that occasion, but I never talked to him, never throughout this period, and throughout this period of my testimony, I had never talked to him. I had talked to the late Badza. We were on quite good terms, and I never had an occasion to talk with Mr. Stanisic. I only saw him there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: At that time did Jovica Stanisic give any speech?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: -- C-015. You said you have met or seen the accused, Stanisic, in Golubic. Do you remember anything that was said either by him or about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was the time when UNPROFOR had forbidden us to have our own army so that we had to have police forces, because in UN protected zones there could be no more troops but the police only. Mr. Stanisic called all of them. The commanders of the police stations were present there in the area where the UN was deployed, and he told them in very nice words how they should conduct themselves. He spoke in professional terms, how they should comport themselves, vis-a-vis the UN, how they should look and behave like policemen, especially those who had been properly schooled and trained. So he said nothing apart from giving them the instructions how they should comport themselves and how they should cooperate with the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: At that meeting that you just described where Stanisic spoke, did anyone else speak at that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Martic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And would you tell the Court what Martic said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, here again this is something that I did not say in my statement, and now he's making me say what he had said. Mr. Judge, do I have to say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you know what Mr. Martic said during that meeting, the Chamber would like to know the answer to the question, which was: What did Mr. Martic say at that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will respect your decision, but this was not the way it was with the statement, but I shall abide by your ruling. Martic said that present with us was his only and first commander, Mr. Jovica Stanisic, called the "icy one," and he gave him the floor then, and then Jovica said what I said before, that he had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever see, at any time, the accused -- either of the accused in the area of the SAO SBWS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us when and where that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the time, but it was in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember roughly when that was? In the early 1990s, in the late 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. It was on two occasions, but I was not present at either of these two meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Do you know with whom Jovica Stanisic met at these occasions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, could we first try to clarify. You were asked whether you ever saw, at any time, the accused, either of the accused, in the area of the SAO SBWS, and then you said, "I saw Jovica Stanisic." A few lines further down, you said when asked when it was, early the 1990s or late 1990s, you say, "I do not remember. It was on two occasions, but I was not present ..." My question is: If you're not present, how can you see someone? This is by any other ways? Did you see it on television? Is it -- what -- how do I have to reconcile your two answers that you saw Mr. Stanisic and, at the same time, that you were not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move into private session and then I will tell you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of June, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.54 p.m.,
